gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured solar-charge result for any candidate. The Gadgeteer measured the Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2's battery climbing from about 30% to above 85% in two days of Texas April sun and then holding at 70–95%. MacRumors measured a Birdfy feeder that never dropped below 90% in a sunny spot while a second Birdfy in a wooded spot sat at about 50%.
standout_why: I opened four of the pages ChatGPT got. Reviewed (2026-11-06) has no battery percentages or day counts for solar charging. It only says the Birdfy Metal 2 'battery stayed consistently charged' and the Harymor 'charged in the sun and was ready to go the next day'. Its measured figures are 78 Harymor notifications in one day and that only one solar panel survived three weeks. Feeder Field says it has 'not used these feeders' and gives spec claims only. Birdfeederlab says it doesn't test products ourselves. The cited WIRED and Good Housekeeping pages blocked automated fetching, so I could not check them. Other secondhand roundups describe WIRED's Kiwibit test only as the solar roof keeping the camera 'charged through a six-week test' with no percentages, so WIRED probably lacks the logged figures, but I have not seen that page myself.
decides: This backs the shopper's premise that a solar feeder can run without manual charging, using numbers from the Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 (the likely '$159.99 Kiwibit 4K solar' card ChatGPT showed) and from Birdfy. It also adds a deciding caveat: placement matters as much as the model. In MacRumors' test, shade cut a Birdfy's steady charge from 90%+ to about 50%. The Gadgeteer warns that frequent 3-minute 4K clips can drain the Kiwibit's battery in under a week even with solar. The page should tell shoppers to mount the feeder in full sun and keep clips short, whichever model they pick. No named reviewer published measured battery figures for the Bird Buddy Pro Solar, the Soliom, or the Birdfy Metal 2 4K, so this cannot decide between those three.
